    ATS Score Checker: What Your Score Actually Means and How to Raise It

    By ATS Score Checker Free Editorial TeamUpdated November 4, 2026 9 min read

    If you have run your resume through an ATS score checker, you have probably seen a number like 64/100 and wondered what to do with it. Is 64 bad? Will an employer reject you automatically? Should you rewrite everything? This guide explains what that score represents, what it does not represent, and a practical order of operations for improving it without turning your resume into a keyword dump.

    What an ATS is, in plain terms

    An Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is the software companies use to collect applications, store candidate data and move people through a hiring pipeline. Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, iCIMS, Taleo and SmartRecruiters are common examples. When you upload a resume, the ATS tries to parse it: it pulls out your name, contact details, job titles, employers, dates, education and skills, and stores them as structured fields that recruiters can search and filter.

    Recruiters then search that database (for example, "product manager" + "SQL" + "Bengaluru") or review applicants for a specific opening. Some systems add knockout questions or a relevance ranking. In most cases, a human still makes the decision — but they only see what the system extracted and surfaced.

    A common myth

    You will often read that "75% of resumes are rejected by ATS before a human sees them." That figure is widely repeated but poorly sourced. The more accurate picture: an ATS rarely 'rejects' you on its own, but a resume that parses badly or lacks the words a recruiter searches for is much easier to overlook.

    What an ATS score checker actually measures

    No checker has access to a particular employer's private configuration, so every ATS score is an estimate of readability and relevance. A good checker looks at the same things that cause trouble in real systems:

    • Parseability — can the text be extracted cleanly, in the right order? Tables, text boxes, multi-column layouts, headers/footers and images are the usual culprits.
    • Section structure — are standard headings present (Experience, Education, Skills, Summary) so the parser knows where each piece belongs?
    • Contact information — is your email and phone number in the body of the document rather than in a header image?
    • Keywords and skills — does the resume use the role-specific terms a recruiter is likely to search for?
    • Content quality — are bullet points specific, action-led and backed by results, or vague and duty-based?
    • Length and density — is there enough substance without being padded?

    Our free ATS score checker scores formatting, wording, structure and readability separately, so you can see where points were lost, not just how many. That breakdown matters more than the total. It does not compare your resume with a job posting, so check role-specific keywords yourself.

    What is a good ATS score?

    Score rangeWhat it usually meansWhat to do next
    80–100Clean structure, relevant keywords, strong bulletsTailor keywords for each job and apply
    60–79Readable, but with weak wording or missing sectionsFix the lowest-scoring category first
    40–59Likely parsing or structure problemsSimplify layout, add standard headings
    Below 40Text may not be extracting correctlyRebuild in a single-column, text-based format

    Treat these bands as guidance. A 72 for a resume tailored to one specific job can be more useful than an 88 for a generic resume that matches nothing in particular.

    Why your score differs between tools

    It is normal to get 58 on one tool and 74 on another. Each tool weights categories differently, some compare against a job description and some do not, and some reward keyword frequency more heavily. The useful habit is to read the specific issues each tool flags. If two different checkers both say "no Skills section detected", that is a real problem. If only one complains about a keyword appearing too rarely, it is a judgement call.

    A step-by-step plan to raise your ATS score

    1. Fix parsing first. Copy your resume text and paste it into a plain text editor. If the order is scrambled, dates are separated from roles, or sections are missing, the ATS is seeing the same mess. Move to a single-column layout and remove tables and text boxes.
    2. Use standard section headings. "Work Experience" beats "Where I've Made an Impact". Creative headings confuse parsers and recruiters skimming quickly.
    3. Put contact details in the body. Name, email, phone, city and LinkedIn URL as plain text at the top — not in the document header or footer.
    4. Match the job description's language. If the posting says "stakeholder management" and you wrote "worked with teams", use their phrase where it is truthful.
    5. Add a focused Skills section. List tools, methods and certifications as plain comma-separated text or short bullet lines.
    6. Rewrite weak bullets. Start with a strong verb, say what you did, and add a measurable result: "Reduced invoice processing time from 5 days to 2 by automating approvals in SAP."
    7. Re-check and compare. Run the updated file through the checker again and confirm the categories you targeted actually improved.

    What not to do

    • Do not paste the job description in white text. Modern systems extract it, and recruiters see it — it looks dishonest.
    • Do not repeat a keyword ten times. Relevance comes from context (the skill used in a real bullet), not raw frequency.
    • Do not list skills you cannot discuss in an interview. Passing the filter only to fail the first call wastes everyone's time.
    • Do not chase 100. Past roughly 85, extra points rarely change outcomes; tailoring and networking do.

    Frequently asked questions

    What is a good score on an ATS score checker?

    Most checkers treat 80 or above as strong, 60–79 as workable with fixes, and below 60 as a sign that parsing or keyword problems are likely. Use the number to prioritise fixes, not as a pass/fail grade.

    Do employers see my ATS score?

    No. Third-party checkers like ours run on your copy of the resume. Employers' systems may rank or filter candidates in their own way, and those internal rankings are not shared with you.

    Why do different ATS checkers give different scores?

    Each tool weights formatting, keywords, sections and content differently. Compare the specific issues each tool flags rather than the headline number.
